doc.title: Ann Rabson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 21, 2007

title: Never wanting another career; teaching herself guitar at Goddard
summary: She never planned anything but music, locked herself in a room at a Vermont camp to teach herself guitar, and describes her percussive Piedmont-style playing.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: That’s great. Was there a point when you were a teenager or whatever, that you really decided I want to be a professional musician?

Oh, that’s a good question. No. There was no time when I thought I was going to do anything else. Well that’s not quite true. When I was, you know I guess I was probably in the seventh grade, sixth grade or seventh grade, I thought maybe I wanted to be a vet or a forest ranger. And there were all these reasons not to be. I couldn’t be a vet because I was a terrible student. I mean my grades, I was lucky — they passed me because my parents were college professors. And I didn’t even show up for school half the time. And the forest ranger, at that time I was told that they don’t hire women as forest rangers, and © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

they probably didn’t. But when I started playing, which wasn’t really until the summer after my sophomore year in high school, I got a guitar. And I’d always wanted to play the guitar. I always wanted to play anything. And I mean I learned the tuning. I locked myself in a room. I was in a camp, a camp in Vermont, at Goddard College, a very sort of radical and leave the kids alone — I locked myself in a room for a month, or maybe it was two months, and I taught myself to play the guitar. I didn’t know that you couldn’t do that. And then when I came out I played gigs. I mean it was like — the same thing happened with the piano. I mean when I decided to learn to play the piano it was not at all long. I mean the first Saffire album that came out, the tape we put out, I had only played piano for a few years. And I still, I mean I can hear that it’s not good but nobody else can. But so many people just love the piano, well and the saxophone of course.

But you have a very muscular style on both your instruments. I don’t know if that’s the exact right word but I just love to watch the way you snap your fingers down on the guitar and it seems — well it works.

I think of it — I pretend that both of them are percussion instruments. But the guitar again, you know, I was listening to Broonzy , I was listening to Lightnin’ Hopkins, Brownie McGhee, you know, these guys. There’s a style of guitar called Piedmont style, which I never would know, but that’s what I was playing. I didn’t realize it until I moved to Virginia and fell in with all these people who played Piedmont guitar. But yeah, I do play, I guess it’s — you know I’m kind of ambidextrous. That doesn’t hurt. I really don’t think it hurts. And it allows me to have strength in both hands.
